doc.title: Bobby Hutcherson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Influences, Los Angeles scene and technique
title: Curtis Amy, Frank Butler and Marilyn Monroe at the Renaissance
summary: Playing One More Ham Hog Please when Marilyn Monroe walked in, and Frank Butler's telephone-book drumming.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: When I look at your discography, I see the name Curtis Amy. Most people don’t know who Curtis was. Could you talk about him?
Great, Curtis Amy was great. Curtis Amy played tenor saxophone. Most of his songs – he wrote a lot of songs, funky type songs that were a lot of fun. One More Ham Hog Please.

I was working with Curtis Amy, Carmell Jones, Frank Butler – ooo, Frank Butler – at the Renaissance, opposite Lenny Bruce. We’re playing. It’s the end – kind of the end of the night. Nobody’s in there. All of a sudden Marilyn Monroe walks in with her entourage, and we’re playing One More Ham Hog Please. Curtis, he just loved to play, and Frank’s playing. Frank is one of these persons, he didn’t miss the scene. Anything happened, he checked it out right away. Curtis too. Eyes would be – first he sees these two blondes walk in, and then the one right behind. All of a sudden, Frank Butler says, “That’s Marilyn Monroe.” The band says [Hutcherson sings four notes], and the band stopped. Marilyn Monroe turned around with a big smile. She says, “Oh, don’t stop. Please keep playing.” Um-um. We all ran over to the table and had to go over and say hello. The music stopped. We ran right. Oh man, Marilyn Monroe. “Please go back up and play.” So we all go back. Curtis had a – always played with a hat on, because he had a bald head with an indention in it. He was a lot of fun to play with. And Frank Butler – Frank Butler was the only drummer who could come to a rehearsal or come to a gig without a set of drums, put a telephone book in front of the chair, play with his fingers on a telephone book, and make you think he had a full set of drums. He could take and roll his fingers on this telephone book, a press roll, with more force than Art Blakey.

And it would be continuous. He – brrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, like that. You say, are you serious? Brrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr. He was something. So we’re back playing. We got back up on the stage and started playing when Marilyn Monroe was there. They got up to walk out, and the band stopped. We had to go see from the backside. The whole band stopped. We had to check it out from the backside. Whoo. Boy, it was happening, boy, yeah. Then Lenny Bruce came. Lenny Bruce, he had to say a whole bunch of stuff about Marilyn Monroe walking out, how she – he said, “Do you see how she locked those knees when she – bam, bam, bam, bam, boom, boom, boom, boom.” It was bad. I used to go over to Elmo Hope’s house, Elmo and Bertha.
